Nov 23 : New Zealand Rugby gave its full backing to All Blacks coach Dave Rennie on Monday despite a first loss to Wales in 73 years and a 37-12 thrashing at the hands of England in the Nations Championship over the last two weekends. Rennie has won seven of 12 tests since taking over in March in the wake of Scott Robertson's departure halfway through his contract following a poor review of the 2025 All Blacks season.  "I've told Dave that and I'm happy to state that publicly that he has our full support," NZR boss Steve Lancaster told Radio New Zealand from England on Monday. "We're confident that we have the right person coaching this team, no question in our minds.

"I've had the benefit of being in this team environment over the course of this year and they're a very strong and aligned group. There's clear leadership. The team are behind Dave, but they know what they have to achieve. "The last two weeks' performance is really disappointing and we need to understand how that's come to pass, but no question over Dave being the right person to lead the team." Lancaster said all the signs pointed to progress being made in the All Blacks set-up less than a year before they head to Australia looking for a fourth World Cup triumph.  "In terms of what we're seeing within the team environment, within the way the team is performing, notwithstanding the last two weeks, which we're absolutely going to have to own and understand, we've seen some positive shifts," Lancaster added.  Lancaster accepted that the tour of South Africa in August and September might have taken too much out of the All Blacks players.     "We probably, neither ourselves nor South Africa, fully appreciated just how gruelling that ... series was," he said. "Those four tests were unbelievable in their intensity, the quality of the rugby, but South Africa have lost their last two matches, three of their last four and we've lost our last two. "We will have to look deeper to understand whether that has been a factor or not, and if it has, what we need to change to ensure that we don't see that again." Fortunately for Rennie and the All Blacks, they have a chance to make immediate amends for their loss to England when they return to Twickenham for the Nations Championship third-place playoff against Steve Borthwick's side on Saturday.      "There's no lack of resolve or motivation," said Lancaster.  "There wasn't going into last week either, right? So that's kind of what makes it a little bit inexplicable, but the team will absolutely be doing everything they can to get up and finish the year on a positive note."

Source: Reuters

BARCELONA, Nov 22 : Diego Simeone has celebrated more dramatic victories during his storied Atletico Madrid tenure, but Sunday's 3-0 win over Getafe secured another landmark as he surpassed Luis Aragones for the most LaLiga victories by a manager. The Argentine's 345th LaLiga win came in his 567th match, 189 fewer than former Atletico boss Aragones needed to reach 344. Yet Simeone's influence on Atletico extends far beyond the numbers. Other managers can boast higher win percentages and larger trophy cabinets, yet Simeone stands alone for longevity, consistency and resilience at the top level of Spanish football. The eight trophies Atletico have won under Simeone would have surpassed the expectations of even the most optimistic supporter when he took charge of a struggling side almost 15 years ago.

The two Champions League final defeats remain the deepest scars of his reign. Both came against city rivals Real Madrid, one on penalties and the other in extra time after Atletico conceded a stoppage-time equaliser. The manner of those losses would have persuaded many managers to walk away. Simeone instead returned undiminished. Dressed in black and gesticulating furiously on the touchline, he displays the same compelling blend of frenetic energy and grim resolve as when he arrived at Atletico in 2011. "It makes me happy," Simeone said of the record after the victory over Getafe. "I don’t usually find many things to be happy about, but there is an incredible amount of work behind this." CONSTANT CRITICISM What has changed is the football. Simeone's teams have evolved considerably over the years, even if he is still forced to confront familiar criticism of his approach. "Then there’s the constant criticism we face. I don’t place much value on it, but I do take note of it," Simeone told Spanish television channel Movistar. "This narrative that we’re a defensive team, as if we’re always playing solely to defend. You don’t win 345 matches just by defending. Is that even possible?" Under Simeone, Atletico have established themselves unequivocally as the third force in Spanish football, disrupting the dominance of Real Madrid and Barcelona. The record has passed from one Atletico great to another, 22 years after Aragones recorded his final LaLiga victory in 2004. Simeone's trajectory suggests his mark could stand for even longer. However long the record survives, his imprint on Atletico and Spanish football is already indelible.

Source: Reuters

Nov 22 : AI developers should adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use "perplexity" as a common metric for measuring AI progress across the industry, OpenAI's chief scientist said on Sunday in a proposal backed by CEO Sam Altman. The proposal detailed by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a blog post was unveiled at a time of growing concern inside and outside the industry about the potential risks of AI's rapidly growing capabilities. "I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone," Pachocki wrote. Pachocki described perplexity as a model intelligence metric concerning how well a model predicts the next token — the basic unit of data — on average, and wrote that lower perplexity means better predictions.

Pachocki wrote that AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027, potentially accelerating progress more quickly than advances in monitoring and safety. Developers should commit to not cross agreed capability thresholds until new monitoring and safety mechanisms are in place, Pachocki said. Pachocki advocated for an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, and defines what milestones must be met before that limit is exceeded. Altman backed the proposal, saying in a post on X that the industry should seek agreement on common limits for AI development. Altman described Pachocki's essay as "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," and said such limits would help ensure safety and control.

Nov 22 : Francesco Pio Esposito's hat-trick was not enough for Inter Milan to secure victory as Atalanta snatched a 4-4 draw at home with a stoppage-time penalty on Sunday, leaving the visitors third in Serie A. Inter moved to 29 points from 12 matches, three behind leaders Lazio and one adrift of second-placed AS Roma, while Atalanta stayed 12th on 15 points. With both Rome clubs winning on Saturday, Inter needed victory to keep pace at the top. Lazio cruised to a 3-0 home win over Lecce, while Donyell Malen struck four times as Roma thrashed Parma 5-1 to preserve their unbeaten Serie A season. Esposito opened the scoring in the 16th minute, finishing from close range after Nicolo Barella's shot was deflected into his path. The 21-year-old doubled the lead in the 32nd, escaping his markers to head Federico Dimarco's corner past Marco Sportiello.

Eljif Elmas pulled one back for Atalanta in the 35th minute, but Esposito restored Inter's two-goal advantage in the 52nd, running onto a perfectly timed through ball from Marcus Thuram and finishing with ease. Charles De Ketelaere renewed Atalanta's hopes in the 72nd minute, only for Petar Sucic to make it 4-2 for Inter from the penalty spot four minutes later. The hosts refused to relent and De Ketelaere struck again in the 80th minute to set up a tense finish. Franck Kessie delivered the final twist, calmly converting a stoppage-time penalty after an Alessandro Bastoni handball to complete Atalanta's comeback. MILAN HIT FIVE TO GO FOURTH AC Milan overtook Como to reclaim fourth place on 27 points with a 5-1 home victory over Frosinone earlier on Sunday. Adrien Rabiot helped create both of Milan's first-half goals. Gabriele Calvani diverted his pass into his own net in the fourth minute, before Goncalo Ramos converted another Rabiot delivery from close range in the 19th. Patrizio Masini replied for Frosinone in the 25th after the ball broke to him in a crowded penalty area. Leading 2-1 at halftime, Ruben Amorim's side pulled clear through substitutes Ardon Jashari and Alphadjo Cisse, who scored in the 48th and 60th minutes. Cisse's effort was initially disallowed before a VAR review overturned the decision. Christian Pulisic added Milan's fifth in the 68th, carrying the ball from his own half and lifting his finish over Frosinone keeper Lorenzo Palmisani. WOLTEMADE SPARKS JUVENTUS SECOND-HALF ROUT Juventus marked coach Luciano Spalletti's 600th Serie A match with a 4-0 home win over Venezia, scoring all four goals in an 18-minute burst after the interval. They climbed to sixth on 21 points, leaving Venezia on six at the bottom of the table. Spalletti brought on Nick Woltemade at halftime with the match goalless, and the German soon had a hand in two goals. He seized on the loose ball from a blocked Weston McKennie shot to score in the 53rd minute, then supplied Teun Koopmeiners for the second six minutes later. An Edon Zhegrova cross brought the third in the 65th minute, with Juan Cabal heading in. Randal Kolo Muani won and converted a penalty six minutes later to complete the second-half rout. “In the first half, we gave the ball away too cheaply, there was nobody moving from their positions, nobody following the flow of the pass, so it was fundamental the players recognised we were missing something, which we provided in the second half," Spalletti said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON/BOSTON: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday (Nov 22) that it would be difficult for him to work with Senator Chuck Schumer if the Democrat is elected Senate majority leader. "It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst [in] history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again."    Schumer, a New York Democrat, is currently minority leader in the Senate but Democrats next year will take control of both chambers of Congress after sweeping wins in midterm elections earlier this month.  Despite the midterm wins, Schumer faces dissatisfied progressives who say a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers needs new leadership.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is making a bid for the Senate leadership, although Schumer has said he has the votes to continue as leader. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for next month.  After the elections , Trump appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to run the White House , suggesting the president will take an even more confrontational approach in his last two years in office. But Trump also has hinted he might work with Democrats on issues such as healthcare. Speaking on CNN on Sunday, Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said she supported expanding Medicare to cover all Americans. "If we have to call it TrumpCare in order to get it across the finish line, that's fine by me," she said. Flanagan said she would support Van Hollen for majority leader. "What we heard from voters is that they were pushing back against the status quo," Flanagan said.

CALGARY, Canada, Nov 22 : Focusing on the legacy of the Women's World Cup should be the top priority for those organising the 2031 and 2035 tournaments, according to a sports executive behind the 2023 competition. In Zurich on Monday, FIFA will confirm that the United States, Jamaica, Costa Rica and Mexico will host in 2031, with England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland on co-hosting duties in 2035. Unlike Australia and New Zealand in 2023, there will be 48 teams rather than 32, streaming giant Netflix will have some involvement and the tournaments will be held in markets more mature in terms of women's soccer development than Australia. But for James Johnson, who was the CEO for Football Australia between 2020 and 2025 and is now the commissioner of the Canadian Premier League, legacy remains the fundamental driving force administrators should be thinking about.

"If you're focused on legacy, I think it helps the tournament," he told Reuters by Zoom from Calgary, Canada, after writing a book on his 2023 experience, "Hosting the World". "In Australia it was about moving the sport from a fourth, fifth or even sixth-tier sport into the mainstream, and we were able to accomplish that. "It is a different market for 2031 and 2035. But the legacy conversation starts as soon as the hosting is officially awarded to those countries." An imperative for Johnson in 2023 was that the Matildas made it to the last weekend of the tournament, something he ensured by fighting for long-term funding for the team. Getting to the third-placed playoff meant many weeks of exposure for women's soccer in a country more traditionally interested in cricket and rugby. 'BETTER OPPORTUNITIES' And although it has received some criticism elsewhere for diluting quality, Johnson believes the expansion to 48 teams for 2031 and 2035 provides an opportunity for the host countries to spend more time in the limelight. "The additional content, the additional matches, what I hope it translates into is better opportunities for the home teams because that's really the amplifier of culture and the amplifier of interest in the tournaments," he said. "A host nation taking the tournament by storm and staying in there from start to finish is a key for the success of the tournament - and the cultural impact you create as a result." Next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil will include the involvement of a major streamer for the first time, with Netflix securing rights in the US and Canada for that tournament and the 2031 competition, as well as expressing interest in the 2030 men's World Cup. Ahead of the 2023 World Cup FIFA were critical of some traditional broadcasters – especially in Europe – for what they said was an undervaluation of women's soccer. But while Johnson welcomed the arrival of Netflix, he cautioned against the long-term danger of locking out potential viewers who had previously watched on free-to-air. "It creates a new dynamic, it's interesting, it's healthy for the sport because there's more competitions," he said. "What I hope it doesn't do though is put too much content behind paywalls because I think the beauty of a World Cup is the community that it creates, and the buzz that it creates, and the ability to bring people together, which means it needs to be widely distributed."

Source: Reuters

Nov 22 : After an eight-year journey, the European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has begun orbiting the solar system's smallest and innermost planet Mercury, though the European Space Agency said on Sunday a glitch has occurred involving its thrusters. Mercury, only slightly larger than Earth's moon, is the least explored of the four planets in the inner solar system, with BepiColombo only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and just the second to orbit it. It is a joint mission of the European Space Agency, or ESA, and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA. ESA confirmed on Saturday that BepiColombo had begun its orbit. In a social media post on Sunday, ESA said the spacecraft had a successful entry into orbit, but during the maneuver, "the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue."

"The spacecraft is safe and teams at ESOC (the European Space Operations Centre) are working to understand what happened," ESA said, adding that "updates will be provided on Monday." The robotic spacecraft, launched in 2018, is a composite of ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, which have different scientific objectives and are due to separate on December 9 and 10. Routine science operations are slated to commence in April. The mission will seek to answer questions about Mercury such as why it has a magnetic field, why ice exists in the polar craters of a sun-scorched planet, and what is the nature of enigmatic depressions called "hollows" on its surface. Mercury's surface looks similar to that of the moon, with numerous impact craters. There are expanses of smooth terrain as well as cliffs, some up to a mile (1.6 km) tall. Mercury is about 60 per cent closer to the sun than Earth. That means that from its surface, the sun appears more than three times as large and seven times as luminous as it does when seen from Earth. Mercury's diameter of 3,032 miles (4,880 km) is less than 40 per cent of Earth's diameter of 7,926 miles (12,753 km).

Source: Reuters
